items.title: Everyday use
items.text:
Open the dashboard at http://localhost:3005 on the Docker host, or replace localhost with the host's address. DUMB starts enabled services in dependency order when the container starts.

On a fresh installation, managed applications are disabled until you choose them in onboarding. The API and frontend provide the setup interface.

items.title: Start, stop, or inspect a service
items.text:
1. Select the service on the dashboard.
  2. Check its status and health reason before taking action.
  3. Use Start, Stop, or Restart. If a downstream media server uses the affected storage, review the playback and library-protection prompt.
  4. Open Service Logs if startup fails, or Tools → Dependencies to inspect missing prerequisites.

Saving a service's configuration and starting it are separate actions. Save to File persists the change; Apply in Memory, where offered, changes only the controller's current configuration. An application may still need a restart or an explicit setup action to use new settings.

Use the service-controls screenshot to find these controls and the log-filter walkthrough to inspect a failure.

items.title: Review updates
items.text:
Use Updates on the dashboard to check enabled services and install selected available updates. For a saved release, branch, commit, or version pin, open that service's Updates panel and review its configured target.

Action Effect Check for updates Refresh version information without restarting the service Install update Install the available target and restart the affected service Install configured release/branch/commit Apply the source selection saved for that service Override + latest Explicitly bypass the saved selection for one install

For scheduled checks, open that service's Tools → Updates, enable Scheduled update checks, and choose Show on dashboard under When available. Set Start time and Interval (hours), then select Save auto-update. Check Next check to confirm a schedule exists. Fixed source selections can disable scheduling; see Auto-update.

Technical alternative: configure scheduled checks with JSON

For scheduled checks, configure each service separately:

{
  "auto_update": true,
  "auto_update_mode": "check_only",
  "auto_update_start_time": "04:00",
  "auto_update_interval": 24
}

This fragment checks daily and reports available updates without installing them. The interval is in hours and the start time uses HH:MM. Settings belong inside the selected service or instance; source pins can disable scheduling. See Auto-update for supported strategies and automatic installation.

The DUMB container itself is updated through your Docker deployment. An available API update notice does not replace the container automatically.

items.title: Stop the container
items.text:
Use your deployment tool's normal stop action. DUMB stops managed processes and unmounts rclone during shutdown.

Technical alternative: set the Compose shutdown grace period

The maintained Compose example allows 30 seconds:

services:
  DUMB:
    stop_grace_period: 30s

Allow active backups, migrations, and restore jobs to finish before stopping DUMB. Closing their browser panels does not stop the backend work.

items.title: Explore the interface
items.text:
Find the screen for your task. Images match the site's light or dark theme. Open any image for a closer look.

Frontend 1.91.0 · DUMB 2.23.0 · Example data, including setup status

items.title: DUMB and application accounts are separate
items.text:
A DUMB account gives operator access to its dashboard, including service and user management. Opening an app inside DUMB does not sign you into that app: Plex, Jellyfin, pgAdmin, and other services may ask for their own account.

See Authentication before sharing DUMB access with someone else.

items.title: If the instructions do not match your screen
items.text:
Check the DUMB and frontend versions in Settings → About, then choose Latest release or Development documentation in this site's header. An older installation may not show a newer tool.

Use a current browser. If the dependency graph's Flow view cannot display, its Details view provides the connections as text.

items.title: What Geek mode adds
items.text:
The normal guides use frontend tools. Geek sections explain the underlying processes and connections, or show alternatives such as API calls, command-line tools, environment variables, and manual configuration.

Geek mode changes these docs; it does not change DUMB's settings. How the documentation modes work.

Geek reference: how the dashboard connects and alternative deployment settings

items.title: Ports and live connections
items.text:
The maintained Compose example publishes the frontend on 3005. Bundled Traefik uses 18080 for service UI routes; it does not replace the frontend listener.

The frontend proxies backend requests under /api and streams status, metrics, and logs over WebSockets. A reverse proxy in front of the dashboard must allow those WebSocket connections. If the connection indicator is disconnected, check proxy and network settings before relying on the displayed sample as current.

items.title: Frontend configuration
items.text:
Managed installations receive these values from DUMB. A separately deployed frontend must use addresses reachable from its own container:

Variable Default Purpose DUMB_API_URL http://127.0.0.1:8000 Backend API DUMB_TRAEFIK_URL API host on port 18080 Embedded HTTP and WebSocket proxy target NUXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED 1 Disable Nuxt telemetry

DUMB injects the current Traefik listener into its managed frontend, including when port reservation moves Traefik away from 18080.

items.title: Browser support
items.text: Use a current Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, Safari, or Edge release. The dependency panel's Flow view uses Mermaid 12 and requires Safari 17.4+ or another ES2024-capable browser. If that view cannot render, use Details to inspect dependencies. See the Mermaid 12 release notes for its browser requirements.

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: The dashboard shows configured services, their health, and start/stop/restart controls. Select a card to open its logs, configuration, and application interface.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The dashboard displays service cards for each configured service, showing:

  • Service name and status
  • Health indicator
  • Auto-restart badge
  • Quick action and available-update buttons
Service Dashboard Read the guide ↗

See which services are running and open the app you need.

View full size ↗

Frontend 1.91.0 · DUMB 2.23.0 · Example data.

items.title: Service cards
items.text: Each service is represented by a card with the following elements:

items.title: Status indicator
items.text: Color Status  Green Running and healthy  Amber Running but degraded  Blue Application is starting or migrating  Rose Running but application health is unhealthy  Red Stopped  Gray Unknown status

items.title: Health badge
items.text:
When a service has health checks enabled, you'll see:

  • Healthy - Service is responding correctly
  • Degraded - Application is reachable but reports a warning
  • Starting - Application is initializing or migrating
  • Unhealthy - Application failed a restart-relevant health check

Hover the indicator or health badge to see the probe, reason, and component states supplied by the backend. The sidebar's Unhealthy filter includes only restart-relevant unhealthy states, not degraded or starting services.

items.title: Auto-restart badge
items.text:
If auto-restart is enabled for a service:

  • Shows restart count (e.g., "Restarts: 2")
  • Indicates the auto-restart feature is active

items.title: Resource badges (Geek Mode)
items.text:
With Geek Mode enabled, each service card shows live resource badges:

  • CPU% - Color-coded by usage (green < 50%, amber < 80%, red >= 80%)
  • Memory RSS - Current resident memory usage
  • DB Healthy/Moderate/High/Critical + score - Current Database Health pressure for services explicitly opted into monitoring, color-coded by severity; hover for provider, mode, score, and recommendation

Metrics are polled every 5 seconds while Geek Mode is active and stop automatically when disabled. Database Health badges are omitted for unsupported services and services whose Database Health monitoring is disabled. Geek Mode never enables collection automatically.

items.title: Quick actions
items.text:
Each service card provides action buttons:

Button Action Description Start Start a stopped service Stop Stop a running service Restart Restart a running service Update Install the version already reported as available

The per-service Update button appears only after DUMB has recorded an ordinary available update. It restarts that service as part of the install. Saved release, branch, commit, and pinned-version choices are never overridden by this shortcut.

Tooltips

Hover over action buttons to see what each will do.

items.title: Check and update multiple services
items.text:
Bulk updates use the dashboard's shared panel. Saved source choices still need an individual review:

flowchart TD
    accTitle: Review and install selected dashboard updates
    accDescr: Check enabled services, review pinned source choices individually and confirm only the available updates you intend to install.
    Open["Open dashboard Updates"] --> Check["Check all"]
    Check --> Rows["Review versions and each service result"]
    Rows --> Source{"Row says Review source?"}
    Source -->|Yes| Individual["Open that service's Updates panel"]
    Source -->|No| Available{"Update available?"}
    Available -->|No| Keep["Keep the current service version"]
    Available -->|Yes| Select["Select the intended available updates"]
    Select --> Confirm["Install selected and confirm restarts"]
    Confirm --> Verify["Review results, health and logs"]

Use Updates in the dashboard header to review every enabled service that supports DUMB-managed updates.

The button shows a pending count when cached checks report available updates. This includes checks run manually and services configured with scheduled Show on dashboard (auto_update_mode: check_only). The dashboard refreshes the inventory periodically while open, so a completed background check can light the badge without reloading the page.

  1. Select Check all to check the services sequentially.
  2. Review current and available versions plus any updater message.
  3. Select some updates, or use Select available.
  4. Select Install selected and confirm the restart warning.

Checks and installs run one service at a time. The panel shows the active service and retains a result on each row. You can close the panel without cancelling the operation: the dashboard shows a background-progress banner, and reopening Updates reattaches to the same progress and row states.

After an install finishes, newer DUMB backends show two measurements on the service row:

  • Install is the complete update operation, including download/cache restore, build, activation, readiness checks, stabilization, and rollback when required.
  • Downtime starts immediately before DUMB stops the old managed process and ends when the replacement first passes its application-readiness probe. The stabilization window after that first ready response remains part of Install, not Downtime. If no running process was stopped, the row says downtime was not observed. A failed update that never regains verified readiness reports a minimum measured downtime and says readiness was not confirmed.

These values use DUMB's monotonic server clock and bounded readiness polling, so they measure the managed service interruption rather than browser request time. The display is gated by the update_timing_metrics backend capability; older backends continue to show normal update results without the timing row.

Only rows in the normal Update available state can be bulk-selected. A row marked Review source has a saved release, branch, commit, or version choice; open that service page to decide whether to install its configured target or use the explicit Override + latest action. The bulk workflow never overrides it.

Checking never restarts a service. Installing does. DUMB Frontend and DUMB API updates are ordered last so the loaded dashboard can report as much progress as possible.

For a DUMB Frontend update, the backend downloads, builds, and validates an adjacent replacement while the current dashboard continues serving requests. It stops the old frontend only for the final atomic swap, restart, and readiness check. The loaded dashboard treats that brief proxy disconnect as expected, reconnects to the backend's retained update status, and reloads itself after the replacement is ready. A failed candidate build leaves the current frontend running; a failed activation restores the previous runtime. DUMB API updates can still interrupt the final inventory refresh because the API is the update control plane itself. After a bulk update, verify service health and logs before continuing normal operation.

items.title: Metrics
items.text: Open Metrics to inspect current resource usage, compare history, and find services consuming CPU, memory, or storage. Choose the filesystems and interfaces visible inside DUMB before interpreting the charts.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The metrics dashboard shows:

  • Real-time gauges - Current resource usage
  • Historical charts - Usage trends over time
  • Process details - Per-service resource consumption
  • Database health - Optional SQL and persistent-store pressure summaries
  • Plex cloud status - Optional cached status for Plex-operated services
  • System information - Container and host details
Container metrics Read the guide ↗

See CPU, memory, storage and network activity.

View full size ↗

Frontend 1.91.0 · DUMB 2.23.0 · Example data.

items.title: CPU usage
items.text:
Metric Description Usage % Current CPU utilization Core Count Available CPU cores Load Average 1, 5, 15 minute averages

The CPU gauge shows:

  • Green: 0-60%
  • Amber: 60-85%
  • Red: 85%+

items.title: Memory usage
items.text: Metric Description Used Currently allocated memory Available Free memory for allocation Total Total system RAM Usage % Percentage in use

items.title: Swap usage
items.text:
Metric Description Used Current swap utilization Total Total swap space Usage % Percentage in use

Swap monitoring

High swap usage may indicate memory pressure. Consider increasing container memory limits.

items.title: Disk usage
items.text:
Metric Description Used Space consumed Free Available space Total Total disk capacity Usage % Percentage in use

Use Metrics → Settings → Monitored Filesystems to choose one or more paths that DUMB can see inside its container. The discovered list includes eligible container mounts; custom absolute container paths are also accepted. For example, if the storage you care about is bind-mounted at /data, select /data rather than /.

Docker does not expose an unmounted host path to DUMB. The selector therefore uses container paths, not host paths. The first selected path is marked Primary and supplies the existing disk/inode history chart and compatibility API fields. Use the arrow controls to change the primary path. All selected filesystems appear in the live card and participate in disk/inode alerts; unavailable paths are shown explicitly.

items.title: Inode usage
items.text:
Metric Description Used / free / total Filesystem entries consumed and remaining Usage % Percentage of available inodes in use

The Filesystems card shows disk and inode pressure for every selected path, plus a zoomable inode-history chart for the primary path alongside system/container I/O. Inodes represent filesystem entries for files and directories, so a filesystem can reach 100% inode usage and reject new files even when byte capacity remains. JSON history exports retain each filesystem entry; CSV exports add disk and inode percentage columns for every path present in the selected history range.

items.title: Network I/O
items.text:
Metric Description Bytes Sent Total outbound data Bytes Received Total inbound data Packets Sent Outbound packet count Packets Received Inbound packet count

Use Metrics → Settings → Monitored Network Interfaces to select every visible interface or a specific set. The default all option preserves the previous aggregate, including loopback. Selecting a specific bridge interface such as eth0 removes unrelated loopback traffic from the aggregate rate chart.

The Network card shows the selected aggregate plus per-interface link state, speed, MTU, current send/receive rate, cumulative counters, and nonzero error/drop totals. JSON history retains the interface records, and CSV exports add send/receive rate columns for every interface present in the selected range.

Only interfaces visible inside DUMB's network namespace are available. A normally bridge-networked container cannot inspect host interfaces; host interfaces become visible when DUMB runs with host networking.

items.title: Historical charts
items.text:
The metrics page displays time-series charts showing resource usage over time:

  • Time range - Configurable history window
  • Bucket size - Data aggregation interval
  • Auto-refresh - Continuous updates via WebSocket

items.title: Chart controls
items.text: Control Function Zoom Scroll to zoom in/out Pan Click and drag to move Reset Double-click to reset view

items.title: Per-process metrics
items.text:
View resource usage for individual services:

Column Description Process Service name PID Process ID CPU % CPU utilization Memory % RAM utilization Memory RSS Resident set size

Sort by any column to identify resource-intensive services.

items.title: Plex cloud status
items.text:
Enable Plex Cloud Status from Metrics → Settings or open the Plex service page and choose Plex Status. After it is enabled, the Metrics page shows Plex's overall public status, the latest collection time, affected components, active incidents, scheduled maintenance, and links to the official status entry.

The existing Metrics alert banner adds a Plex cloud alert when the enabled feed reports a disruption. A temporary refresh failure shows the last successful sample as Stale instead of replacing it with a false operational state.

This panel is deliberately separate from the local Plex service indicator:

  • Plex service status tells you whether the DUMB-managed Plex process is running and healthy.
  • Plex Cloud Status summarizes infrastructure operated by Plex.

An operational cloud status does not prove that local playback, remote access, DNS, routing, or port forwarding is working. The metric is disabled by default and sends no Plex token or local library/service data.

items.title: Database health
items.text:
Only services explicitly opted into Database Health monitoring appear in the Database Health table on the Metrics page. Supported services with monitoring disabled remain available in Metrics → Settings and the service page's Database Health panel so they can be enabled, but they are omitted from the results table. When no services are monitored, the section shows a concise empty state with a Configure action instead of disabled service rows.

Database health Read the guide ↗

Find monitoring options for a service's database.

View full size ↗

Frontend 1.91.0 · DUMB 2.23.0 · Example data.

The Database Health section appears near the bottom of the live Metrics content. When Plex Cloud Status is enabled, its card follows Database Health; System remains last. Select any column header to sort ascending or descending; size, WAL, signal, pressure, and probe columns sort by their underlying numeric values rather than the formatted text, and unavailable values remain last. The selected sort is retained in that browser. Click or keyboard-activate any service row to expand or collapse its full details. Expanded details match the service-page panel and include the recommendation, score reasons, database paths/names, provider metadata, filesystem capacity, inode pressure, read-only/network state, probe results, and observed log signals. Column headers, settings, status badges, and detail fields include tooltips, and the section links directly to the Database Health documentation.

The table shows:

  • detected SQL provider or custom store format and current pressure classification;
  • combined database/store and SQLite WAL size;
  • database-related log-signal count;
  • bounded read-only probe latency when Enhanced mode is enabled;
  • a service-specific recommendation.
  • filesystem byte usage/free space, inode usage/free inodes, and read-only state in the expanded details.

Use Standard / passive for the lowest overhead. Use Enhanced / read-only probes when you need SQLite page/WAL metadata or PostgreSQL statistics. Plex is always collected passively while running, even if Enhanced is selected. Decypharr append-log stores, Phalanx DB Hyperbee data, and the Zurg state directory are also passive-only; Enhanced does not open or query those formats.

The supported set includes the Arrs, InfiniDysk, Bazarr, Plex, CLI Debrid/Battery, Emby, Jellyfin, Profilarr, Tautulli, AltMount, Pulsarr, Seerr, PostgreSQL, pgAdmin, Riven Backend, Zilean, Traefik Proxy Admin, Decypharr, Phalanx DB, and Zurg. DUMB detects SQLite versus PostgreSQL for provider-neutral services and keeps multi-instance entries separate.

Enable Ignore network storage score for an individual service when its NFS/SMB placement is intentional. The filesystem remains visible in the service details, but it no longer raises the pressure score or replaces recommendations derived from the remaining metrics.

The override excludes only network placement. Low free space, high inode usage, read-only storage, WAL growth, log errors, probe latency, locks, deadlocks, and long-running transactions continue to affect the result.

Pressure classifications are healthy, observing, moderate, high, critical, unavailable, or disabled. Collect through representative imports, scans, health checks, and playback before deciding whether PostgreSQL would help.

Open How to read Database Health for an in-product explanation of observed signals, score bands, and limitations. Database Health is evidence rather than a benchmark: it cannot profile individual SQL queries, prove root cause, predict an exact provider speedup, guarantee every transient event was captured, repair databases, or replace backups and application-native diagnostics.

items.text:
DUMB automatically detects whether it's running in a cgroup-limited environment (Docker/Kubernetes) and reports metrics accordingly:

  • cgroup mode - Reports container limits, not host resources

items.title: WebSocket connection
items.text:
Metrics are streamed in real-time via WebSocket:

Status Indicator Connected Live updates active Connecting Establishing connection Disconnected No live updates

The frontend automatically reconnects if the connection drops.

items.title: Update interval
items.text:
Open Metrics → Settings to adjust collection and history settings. Change the intended value, select the displayed Apply action, and check that live values/history continue updating.

Configure how frequently metrics are updated:

Setting Default Range Interval 2 seconds 0.5-10 seconds

Lower intervals provide more responsive updates but increase network traffic.

items.title: History settings
items.text: Setting Default Description Retention 7 days How long to keep history Bucket Size 5 seconds Aggregation interval History read backend SQLite Serve history from local SQLite or optional DUMB-managed PostgreSQL Max local SQLite size 100 MB Bounds the compressed local history/continuity payloads SQLite continuity path /config/metrics/metrics.sqlite Persistent local history database and PostgreSQL write-ahead continuity buffer

items.title: History storage status
items.text:
Open Metrics → Settings → History Storage to see:

  • the configured and currently active provider;
  • whether automatic SQLite fallback is active;
  • local and PostgreSQL sample counts and allocated size;
  • the local compressed-to-original JSON ratio;
  • retained legacy JSONL files and import state;
  • the latest safe PostgreSQL connection error.

SQLite is the default local history store. PostgreSQL is an optional alternative for history reads; DUMB keeps local history available if PostgreSQL is temporarily unavailable.

Technical details: PostgreSQL history and SQLite continuity

PostgreSQL is not merely a backup. When selected, synchronized, and healthy, it is the active history query and retention backend. SQLite is written first as a bounded write-ahead continuity buffer so live charts remain available when PostgreSQL is stopped or restarting. Retained local samples are replayed when PostgreSQL reconnects.

On current backends, choosing PostgreSQL only changes the draft selection. The panel explicitly prompts the user to click Apply & activate PostgreSQL; nothing is provisioned until that button is used. Apply enables PostgreSQL if necessary, creates the dedicated database, starts or reuses the managed process, synchronizes retained samples, and switches history reads without restarting DUMB. During the operation the panel displays activation progress. Afterward, a persistent PostgreSQL cutover complete notice confirms that PostgreSQL is serving history reads while SQLite remains the continuity buffer.

If any step fails, the panel keeps SQLite active and returns to the pending state so Apply & activate PostgreSQL can be used to retry. For backward compatibility, dmbdb shows Apply plus restart guidance instead when the connected backend does not advertise hot activation support.

Use Import JSONL now to force a fresh scan for history created by older DUMB releases. The import is timestamp-idempotent, detects files added after an earlier completed migration, and does not delete the source files. Refresh / probe performs an operator-requested PostgreSQL connection test without waiting for the normal retry interval.

See Metrics history storage for configuration, sizing, migration, fallback, and rollback details.

items.title: Alert thresholds
items.text:
Configure when alerts appear on the dashboard:

Resource Default Setting Location CPU 85% Metrics header warning controls Memory 85% Metrics header warning controls Disk 90% Metrics header warning controls Inodes 90% Metrics header warning controls Database Health Off; selectable Moderate/High/Critical minimum Metrics header or Metrics Settings Database Health Monitoring

Alerts appear as banners when thresholds are exceeded and on the global Metrics indicator. DB health / Include Database Health in alerts is optional and browser-local; enabling it does not enable collection for any service or alter its pressure score.

These browser alerts are separate from backend notifications. Backend notifications continue operating without an open browser and have their own persistent thresholds, cooldowns, recovery handling, and delivery history.

Technical alternative: query metrics through the API

items.title: API access
items.text:
Metrics are also available via the REST API:

# Current metrics snapshot
curl http://localhost:3005/api/metrics

# Historical metrics newer than a Unix timestamp
curl "http://localhost:3005/api/metrics/history?since=1784300000&limit=5000"

# Storage, migration, and fallback status
curl "http://localhost:3005/api/metrics/history/storage?probe_postgresql=true"

# Database health, optionally forcing a fresh collection
curl "http://localhost:3005/api/metrics/database-health?process_name=InfiniDysk&refresh=true"

See the WebSocket API documentation for real-time streaming.

items.title: Metrics not updating
items.text:
• Check WebSocket connection status
  • Verify browser supports WebSocket
  • Check for network/firewall issues

items.title: High memory usage
items.text:
• Review per-process metrics to identify heavy services
  • Consider disabling unused services
  • Increase container memory limits

items.title: Disk filling up
items.text:
• Check log file sizes
  • Review metrics retention settings
  • Clear old data if needed

items.title: Onboarding
items.text:
Onboarding selects services, collects their settings, and starts the chosen stack. It opens on a fresh installation; use Settings → Onboarding → Launch Onboarding to run it again.

Existing application data is retained, but the wizard can apply new settings. Use a service's own configuration editor for an ordinary setting change. Onboarding is not a database or namespace migration.

items.title: Before you begin
items.text: Have the intended storage mounted inside DUMB, provider credentials ready, and a plan for which application owns requests, downloads, imports, and playback. A host-only mount or browser-reachable URL may not be visible from inside the container.

items.title: Wizard steps
items.text:
Plan the complete workflow, then check the applications after they start:

flowchart TD
    accTitle: From service selection to a working media workflow
    accDescr: Resolve preflight blockers, review the intended setup, start applications and then verify their accounts, connections, imports and playback.
    Apps["Choose workflow apps and companions"] --> Check["Run preflight checks"]
    Check --> Allowed{"Blocking checks resolved?"}
    Allowed -->|No| Correct["Correct the reported problem"]
    Correct --> Check
    Allowed -->|Yes| Inputs["Enter provider details and installation choices"]
    Inputs --> Review["Review services, paths and requested changes"]
    Review --> Apply["Apply the setup"]
    Apply --> Start["Follow startup results and service logs"]
    Start --> Finish["Finish app accounts and connections"]
    Finish --> Test["Test an import and playback"]

items.title: Step 1: Choose servicesChoose services
items.text:
Select your workflow applications and supporting services, or use Guided setup:

  1. Choose Debrid, Usenet, or Both.
  2. For Usenet, choose Decypharr, InfiniDysk, AltMount, or a supported combination.
  3. Decide whether to use Arrs; Usenet arrangements require them.
  4. Choose Combined or Separate Arr instances when using several workflows.
  5. Optionally choose separate quality-tier Sonarr/Radarr instances.
  6. Select supporting services and choose Apply recommendations.
Layout Result Combined One Arr instance can use several core_service values Separate Independent Arr instances per workflow Multi-quality Additional Sonarr/Radarr instances per quality tier

A tier name such as 1080p is an instance label, not proof that the application has the intended quality profile.

Read the guide ↗

Choose the apps you want DUMB to set up.

items.text:
The wizard checks whether DUMB can continue setup and shows any problems it finds. Read each result, correct blocking errors, then run the check again before continuing.

Resolve blocking failures before continuing. A passed API response does not independently prove that a configured storage path is mounted or usable by another application.

items.title: Skipping onboarding
items.text:
Use onboarding for the guided setup. If you leave before finishing, open Settings → Onboarding → Launch Onboarding to return. Keep track of unfinished provider, account, library, and connection steps; a running service may still need them.

Technical alternative: configure services without the wizard

Set the appropriate enabled flags and required paths/credentials through the service configuration or runtime configuration. Disabled applications will not start merely because their files already exist. Do not skip setup steps by guessing a generated API key or database selector.

Technical details: saved configuration and deployment overrides

items.title: Configuration applied
items.text: The wizard updates the runtime dumb_config.json, including enabled services, selected provider inputs, service options, and instances. Higher-priority environment or secret values still apply. See configuration precedence.

items.title: Multi-instance support
items.text: Instances need distinct names, process identities, ports, and appropriate data paths. Combined Arr layouts can use list-based core_service; separate layouts keep independent integrations. Review the multi-instance guide before changing a working topology.

items.title: After onboarding
items.text:
Check service status, actual application configuration, and one intended end-to-end workflow. Configure media-library protection before unattended storage maintenance, and keep application data backed up.

Setup complete Read the guide ↗

items.title: Service pages
items.text: Select a service card to open its status, configuration, logs, and application interface. Frequent controls stay in the command bar; less frequent tools are grouped under Tools, beside the tab strip. The tools shown depend on the service and connected backend.

items.title: Choose a task
items.text: Task Control Start, stop, or restart Command bar Change DUMB-managed settings DUMB Config Edit the application's configuration Service Config, when available Read or download logs Service Logs, when available; otherwise sidebar Realtime Logs Open the application's own UI Embedded UI Check/install an update Tools → Updates Inspect a missing dependency Tools → Dependencies Diagnose with selected evidence AI Assist Change the page's default tab Tools → Preferences

items.title: Status and controls
items.text:
The header shows process status, application health, and restart information. Hover a health badge for the backend's probe reason. Starting and Degraded are distinct from a restart-relevant Unhealthy result.

Service controls Read the guide ↗

Check a service's status and find its start, stop and restart controls.

View full size ↗

Frontend 1.91.0 · DUMB 2.23.0 · Example data.

Use Start, Stop, or Restart for the current service. The DUMB API page has no start/stop/restart buttons. A storage operation affecting a protected media server prompts for playback and scan handling before it runs. Dashboard bulk updates use safe mode; use the individual service page to review an override.

Save to File persists a configuration. Its DUMB Config split-button also offers Apply in Memory for a temporary controller change. Saving configuration does not necessarily restart or reconfigure the application.

items.title: InfiniDysk namespace migration
items.text:
An eligible legacy NzbDAV installation shows its retained migration notice. Choose compatibility-only branding or run the complete namespace preflight. A fresh canonical InfiniDysk installation does not receive this action.

The full cutover requires a current preflight and downtime acknowledgements. It shows a persistent background job with Open progress; navigation or browser refresh reattaches to that job. Restarting DUMB interrupts the job rather than resuming it automatically.

Result Next action Completed Perform the post-migration checks, including paths, scans, and sample playback Failed and rolled back Verify the legacy stack before retrying Interrupted / rollback attention required Preserve the named backup and follow the reported targeted recovery; do not toggle providers or move paths manually

Review cleanup, where offered after success, is an irreversible purge of migration recovery/history data. Keep independent backups and complete validation before using it. See the namespace migration procedure and cleanup instructions.

items.title: Reset / Remove
items.text:
Reset DUMB configuration disables the target and restores its DUMB defaults. Remove service files additionally removes the exact managed paths listed in its preview. The dialog identifies retained/shared paths and requires the exact process name.

Neither operation is a database reset or media-library cleanup. Read Service reset and removal, especially for database-backed services and dependencies.

items.title: Rclone Optimizer tab
items.text:
Eligible InfiniDysk-backed rclone instances show file selection, safety limits, background progress, candidate results, and apply/rollback controls. The production mount supplies discovery metadata; test reads use isolated shadow mounts and can consume provider traffic.

Set limits for your own hardware, connection budget, and provider. A winning profile is a combined result, not proof that each flag is independently optimal. Missing matched provider evidence is shown as unavailable. Apply/rollback interrupts rclone and verifies mount replacement. Use Rclone Streaming Optimizer before starting a test.

items.title: mediastorm first-login credential
items.text: On supported backends, a masked credential notice appears while mediastorm's bootstrap credential file exists. Reveal/copy it only as needed. Current builds require a replacement password during first login; pinned older builds may require changing it immediately after sign-in. The notice disappears when the bootstrap file is removed. See mediastorm setup.

items.title: Database Migration panel
items.text:
Supported services expose Database Migration through backend capability metadata. The panel separates preflight, rehearsal, guarded cutover, and rollback. A successful rehearsal is required before the frontend enables cutover.

Closing the panel does not cancel the backend job. Reopen it to follow progress. InfiniDysk failures, interruption, or rollback problems retain a recovery banner after navigation and reload; use the reported guarded rollback rather than manual provider/file changes.

The SQLite-to-PostgreSQL guide lists supported applications, schema checks, backup requirements, and the limits of rollback.

items.title: Dependency graph view
items.text:
Open Tools → Dependencies to inspect startup order, missing prerequisites, and relationship signals. Available Fix now actions start the identified dependency; review the target before using them.

View Shows Runtime scope Hard runtime and explicitly configured dependencies All scope Runtime edges plus soft/optional application links Details Dependency reasons and current states Flow Mermaid graph and parallel prerequisite groups

Instance links are scoped to the current workflow. An unrelated rclone or Zurg instance is not treated as a valid dependency when the intended mapping is missing. Conditional startup dependencies apply only when the relevant services are enabled. Signals distinguish runtime waits, configured core_service links, and optional integrations.

Open the demonstration.

See which services an app needs before it can start. DUMB 2.23.0 · Frontend 1.91.0 · Example data.

With Geek Mode, the panel also exposes API latency, Copy JSON, and raw Mermaid source. Use Details if the browser cannot render Flow.

items.title: Process Metrics panel
items.text: Geek Mode adds a Process Metrics panel with PID, uptime, CPU/RSS, I/O, ports, connection count, configured paths, container resources, and restart history. It fetches on page entry; Refresh requests a new sample.

items.title: Database Health panel
items.text:
Supported services expose Database Health independently of Geek Mode. Choose Standard / passive or Enhanced / read-only probes explicitly for the intended service. Opening the panel does not enable collection.

Expanded results include provider/store information, pressure reasons, database/WAL size, filesystem capacity and inodes, network/read-only state, log signals, and bounded probe results where supported. Plex while running, Decypharr append logs, Phalanx Hyperbee, and Zurg state remain passive-only.

Ignore network storage score excludes only intentional network placement; low space, inodes, read-only storage, and other signals still count. The panel does not run maintenance, repairs, integrity checks, or migration. See Database Health for interpretation and limits.

items.title: Auto-restart policy
items.text:
Use Tools → Auto-restart to select the current service and set its policy. Global defaults and per-service overrides control the interval, failure threshold, restart window, explicit backoff delays, and grace period.

Monitoring pauses during stack startup. A restart is counted as successful only after the service passes its health check. Starting and Degraded states remain visible without incrementing the unhealthy threshold. See Auto-restart before changing limits.

Use the auto-restart controls walkthrough to locate the policy before changing and saving it.

items.title: Auto-update settings
items.text:
Action Use it to Check for updates Refresh available version/source information without installing Install update Apply the reported available update Install configured release/branch/commit Install the saved source target without overriding it Override + latest Bypass saved source/version selectors for one install

The automatic schedule has an enable switch, start time in HH:MM, interval in hours, and—on supported backends—Show on dashboard or Install automatically. Saving reschedules the updater; fixed source selections can disable scheduling.

Checks and installs keep progress when you close their panel or navigate within the app. A background banner reopens the active result. DUMB Frontend updates build a candidate while the current frontend remains running, then briefly disconnect during activation. The page reconnects, reads the backend's retained result, and reloads after confirmed success. An unconfirmed reconnect asks you to review stored status.

Where update_timing_metrics is supported, Install measures the full operation and Downtime measures from stopping the old managed process to verified application readiness. The DUMB API's release notice never replaces the Docker container automatically.

Auto-update explains source strategies and protection prompts. Install cache covers the dashboard's capability-gated cache usage and cleanup tools.

items.title: Seerr Sync panel
items.text: On Seerr pages, Tools → Seerr Sync configures the primary/subordinate role, polling, external instances, request options, connection tests, and failed-request status. API keys are masked by default. See Seerr Sync for the one-way workflow.

items.title: Edit DUMB Config
items.text:
1. Open DUMB Config for the selected service or instance.
  2. Change the intended fields in the editor. Keep the existing structure and correct any validation errors.
  3. Review the added, changed, and removed settings. Acknowledge highlighted sensitive changes only when intended.
  4. Select Save to File to keep the change after DUMB restarts. Apply in Memory, when offered, is temporary.
  5. Reopen the tab to confirm the saved value. Follow the service guide for any required restart/setup action, then check its health and logs.

Invalid JSON or validation errors block saves. Command, path, credential, and networking changes can require acknowledgement.

On the DUMB API page, DUMB API Logging can temporarily enable DEBUG without a restart when supported. It shows configured/effective levels and clears the override on container restart. It does not change application log levels. If DEBUG is configured persistently, edit the saved configuration to disable it.

items.title: Edit Service Config
items.text:
1. Open Service Config when the application provides this tab.
  2. Change the intended application setting and select Save Service Config.
  3. Reopen the editor to confirm the saved value. Follow the application's restart/setup instructions and verify the result in its own interface.

Application settings and DUMB-managed settings are separate. Use the service guide to find the correct editor and restart requirements.

Compare the two tabs in the configuration-editor walkthrough before choosing which setting to change.

items.title: AI Assist
items.text:
1. Choose a diagnostic preset and time/comparison window.
  2. Select Preview bundle to inspect redacted evidence without a provider call.
  3. Select Analyze when ready to send that evidence.
  4. Review coverage and confidence before acting on the response.

Saved provider profiles are shared with Stack AI Assist. Keys stay server-side. Editing a profile's details marks it unsaved; selecting a different provider does not silently overwrite the saved profile. Deep scans inspect retained backend logs within the configured MiB budget, rather than only the visible log rows.

The AI Assistant guide covers supported models, provider setup, redaction, and evidence limitations.

items.title: Logs
items.text:
1. Open Service Logs for the app you want to check.
  2. Choose a log level or enter search text to focus on the relevant lines.
  3. Select Refresh now for a new sample, or choose an interval such as Every 5s for repeated checks. Choose Off to pause those checks.
  4. Keep Follow tail checked to scroll to the newest lines. Download a snapshot when you need to keep it.

You can also change the line limit. Service-aware parsing retains application timestamps/severity and groups multiline errors where supported. Traefik offers access logs; Plex offers DBRepair logs when enabled.

DUMB applies its sensitive-data redactor to logs viewed or downloaded here. Review a download before sharing it; arbitrary application output can contain values the redactor does not recognize.

Open the demonstration.

Filter a service's messages and pause refresh to read them at your own pace. DUMB 2.23.0 · Frontend 1.91.0 · Example data.

items.title: Embedded UI
items.text:
Enable service UIs in Settings, then open the service's Embedded UI tab. Choose its supported base path, use split/full-window view, or open the direct link. A matching enabled TPA HTTPS route can supply a public link; otherwise use the local/private link.

DUMB login does not replace the application's own login. Root-relative APIs, assets, and WebSockets use the frontend's service context. Authelia login and TPA admin SSO open at their public HTTPS origins in a top-level tab.

Sonarr inside DUMB Read the guide ↗

Use Sonarr inside DUMB without changing browser tabs.

View full size ↗

Frontend 1.91.0 · DUMB 2.23.0 · Example data.

items.title: Service workers and browser notifications
items.text: Embedded workers are scoped to the owning service to preserve background updates and destination routing. This routing does not isolate the applications' cookies, CacheStorage, or other storage on the shared frontend origin. Native OS notification delivery also depends on browser and system permissions. A dedicated application origin keeps its own native worker behavior.

items.title: Jellyfin and Emby libraries
items.text:
Sign in within Embedded UI using an application account allowed to access the libraries. A login at the direct server address may not carry over to the frontend origin. If the same account sees libraries directly but not embedded, update the frontend and reopen the tab; older proxies could incorrectly route library requests under the web client's asset path.

See Embedded service UIs for routing and troubleshooting.

items.title: Default tab selection
items.text: Use Tools → Preferences to choose the default tab, or make the current tab the default. On narrow screens, swipe the tab bar horizontally; edge chevrons indicate hidden tabs.

items.title: Sidebar operator QoL
items.text:
Use quick status filters, service/config-key search, saved views, compact mode, or Ctrl/Cmd + K to find a service. The command palette also supports capturing an assigned service shortcut. Auto-hide on navigation is enabled by default and can be disabled for a persistent desktop sidebar.

Sidebar preferences are saved under dumb.ui.sidebar. Dashboard drag-and-drop writes service_order, which both the dashboard and sidebar use.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Open Settings from the sidebar. Expand a section to change its values. Closing a section changes only the layout; it does not disable the feature.

Sections start expanded and remember their open/closed state in each browser.

Settings Read the guide ↗

Find settings for appearance, connections, access and alerts.

Select Enable embedded service iFrames to add embedded application tabs, direct links, and full-window controls to supported service pages. Disabling it removes dashboard access through those routes; native-port access still depends on your deployment's port mappings.

items.title: Notifications
items.text:
This section requires the backend's notifications capability. It configures outbound delivery that continues without an open browser.

  1. Enable notifications and add an Apprise or generic webhook destination.
  2. Choose minimum severity, event types, and intended enabled services.
  3. Save and test the destination.
  4. Review delivery history if a normal event does not arrive.

The default Warning minimum excludes normal Success events, including successful auto-restarts. Save & test bypasses enable switches and routing filters for that test; it does not prove a normal event matches your rules.

Saved destination URLs and headers stay on the server. A blank secret field preserves its existing value. Apprise normally delivers directly from DUMB to the provider; apprise:// and apprises:// explicitly use an Apprise API server.

Notifications documents events, startup baselining, retries, thresholds, and delivery limitations. Browser-local Metrics banners use separate settings on the Metrics page.

Notifications Read the guide ↗

items.title: Geek ModeAdvanced settings
items.text:
This is a preference in the DUMB dashboard, separate from the Geek mode switch in this documentation site's header. The dashboard preference adds diagnostic controls to the application; the docs switch reveals explanations and alternative methods in these guides.

Open Settings → Advanced → Geek Mode and enable it for extra diagnostic details. Return to a service page to see the additional controls:

Location Additional information Service header Internal config key and process name Dependencies API latency, Copy JSON, and Mermaid source in Flow Process Metrics PID, uptime, CPU/RSS, I/O, listening ports, paths, and restart history Dashboard cards CPU/RSS badges, refreshed every five seconds Supported database services Summary of explicitly enabled Database Health collection

Database Health stays opt-in per service. Geek Mode does not run repair, integrity checks, or migrations.

The dependency-panel example shows its ordinary views. Geek Mode adds the diagnostic controls listed above.

items.title: Authentication providerSign-in provider
items.text:
Choose Local, Hybrid, or OIDC only when supported by the connected API. Hybrid retains local login for recovery. OIDC-only requires an explicit lockout-risk confirmation.

The provider editor supports managed/external Authelia and provider presets including Google, Authentik, Keycloak, Entra ID, Auth0, Okta, ZITADEL, Dex, and generic OIDC. Each external provider needs a web application, client ID/secret, and the exact browser-facing HTTPS callback:

https://dumb.example.com/api/auth/oidc/callback

Opening Settings through localhost or an IP address leaves the callback blank. Enter the real HTTPS FQDN and register the exact value at the provider. Select Check discovery, correct any reported error, then select Save provider. Keep Hybrid mode while testing provider sign-in in a separate private browser window.

For bootstrapped DUMB-managed Authelia, Link managed Authelia creates/reuses a dedicated client and transfers its secret without displaying it. Use the Authelia wizard for bootstrap and route setup.

Provider TLS verification stays enabled by default. Allow private endpoint IPs and Allow HTTP are explicit outbound connection exceptions for a trusted provider; changing presets resets them. The full authentication guide covers claim mapping and provider restrictions.

items.title: Start here
items.text:
DUMB (Distributed Unlimited Media Bridge) runs your chosen media services in one container and gives you a dashboard to configure, monitor, and update them. You can use Debrid, Usenet, or both, with a media server inside DUMB or on another machine.

You choose the services. You do not need to enable the whole catalog.

Use the documentation channel that matches your image: Latest release for stable images or Development for dev. How documentation versions work.

items.title: Choose your deployment guide
items.text:
Start with the guide for your host or management tool:

  • Docker Compose · Portainer · Dockge
  • Unraid · Synology · QNAP · TrueNAS SCALE
  • Windows / WSL2 · Proxmox LXC

Compare deployment options. After deployment, continue below with the dashboard and your chosen workflow.

items.title: Choose a workflow
items.text:
What you want Start with Manage a library with Sonarr or Radarr using Debrid Decypharr Manage a Usenet library with Arr applications InfiniDysk or AltMount; Decypharr also supports native Usenet Use lists, watchlists, or requests with a Debrid workflow Riven or CLI Debrid Run a media server Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby Aggregate sources for Stremio AIOStreams Add tools to an existing stack Browse the service catalog; onboarding can skip core workflow selection

These are starting points, not interchangeable backends. Each service has its own provider support, accounts, and library behavior. Check its guide before choosing.

items.title: From install to first playback
items.text:
Start with one workflow and test a real item from import to playback. The steps below link to the instructions for each stage.
  1. Prepare storage and credentials. Read Before you install.
  2. Deploy DUMB. Choose your host in Deployment.
  3. Open the dashboard. The default address is http://<host>:3005.

  4. Complete onboarding. Select services and enter provider credentials. See Onboarding.

  5. Finish application setup. Configure accounts, indexers, download clients, root folders, and media-server libraries in the selected applications.

  6. Check the workflow. Add a test item through your chosen application, confirm its import, and play it from the media server. A running process alone does not establish this.

items.title: What runs where
items.text:
Technical details: control and media paths 
flowchart LR
    USER([You]) --> FE[Dashboard :3005]
    FE --> API[DUMB controller]
    API --> ARR[Arr applications]
    API --> FLOW[Debrid or Usenet service]
    ARR --> FLOW
    FLOW --> LIB[(Mounts and library paths)]
    LIB --> MEDIA[Plex / Jellyfin / Emby]
    FE -. embedded UI .-> ARR
    FE -. embedded UI .-> FLOW

DUMB installs and coordinates services. Each upstream application still owns its accounts, provider behavior, database, and content decisions. The architecture guide explains the boundaries.

Using a media server outside DUMB?

Plan the shared paths before installation. An external application must see the library and the targets of its symlinks. FUSE submounts may also require Linux mount propagation. See rclone and external consumers.

items.title: Before you install
items.text: Have a host, persistent storage, and credentials for the services you plan to use. DUMB creates its initial configuration at startup; you do not need to write a complete dumb_config.json first.

items.title: Plan the library boundary
items.text:
Choose the layout before configuring host mounts. Seeing the same folder name in two applications does not prove that they can read the same files.

flowchart TD
    Consumers["Where will the library be read?"] --> Inside["Only apps inside DUMB"]
    Consumers --> Container["Another container on this host"]
    Consumers --> Remote["Another machine"]
    Inside --> Normal["Use the normal media bind"]
    Container --> Paths["Match library and symlink target paths"]
    Paths --> FUSE{"Must it see DUMB-created FUSE submounts?"}
    FUSE -->|Yes| Shared["Prepare a shared host mount and propagation"]
    FUSE -->|No| Files["Verify ordinary file and link access"]
    Remote --> Export["Plan an explicit sharing method"]
    Shared --> Test["Verify access from the actual reader"]
    Files --> Test
    Export --> Test

items.title: Choose your platform first
items.text:
These guides explain the installation steps for each platform. Use this page to prepare, then follow your selected guide.

  • Docker Compose · Portainer · Dockge
  • Unraid · Synology · QNAP · TrueNAS SCALE
  • Windows / WSL2 · Proxmox LXC

Compare deployment options.

items.title: Host requirements
items.text:
Requirement Guidance Runtime Docker Engine on Linux, including WSL2; or the native Proxmox LXC helper CPU and memory Start around 2 vCPU and 2 GB RAM for a small stack. This is a planning estimate; source builds, databases, transcoding, and larger service selections need more. Storage Persistent storage for configuration, databases, logs, and library paths; SSD storage is preferable for databases and source builds. User and group Non-root PUID and PGID with access to the host directories. Check them with id -u and id -g. Networking Access to image/package registries and your providers. Publish dashboard port 3005 unless you deliberately change it.

Docker Desktop and external mounts

Docker Desktop does not support the bind mount propagation needed to share DUMB-created FUSE/rclone submounts with containers outside DUMB. For Windows, use Docker Engine inside WSL2. See Docker's propagation documentation.

items.title: Accounts and credentials
items.text:
Selected integration Have this ready Debrid API key for each selected provider Usenet NNTP host, port, username/password, connection limit, and TLS setting Plex Claim/token and server address when the selected integration requires them Private or sponsored GitHub repository A read-capable GitHub token with the access that repository requires Cloudflared A Cloudflare Tunnel token

You only need credentials for the integrations you enable. See integration tokens.

items.title: Persistent directories
items.text:
The maintained Compose layout mounts four host directories. Native LXC uses the same absolute paths directly in the guest.

Path inside DUMB Contents /config DUMB configuration, authentication data, migration jobs, snapshots, and feature state /log DUMB and collected service logs /data Persistent application data. DUMB maps internal paths such as /plex, /postgres_data, and /decypharr into subdirectories here. /mnt/debrid Mounts, generated links, and library paths

Keep these paths when recreating or upgrading the container. Store a separate backup of important configuration and application data; a bind mount alone is not a backup.

Existing installations

Separate direct mounts such as /postgres_data or /plex are legacy or advanced layouts. They can prevent DUMB from creating managed data symlinks. Preserve an existing layout until you have reviewed its migration; do not add those mounts to a new deployment by default.

items.title: Decide who reads the library
items.text:
• Everything inside DUMB: use a normal /mnt/debrid bind mount.
  • External Arr or media-server containers: use matching library and target paths. If they need DUMB-created FUSE/rclone submounts, prepare a shared host mount and use :rshared on DUMB's bind, with the appropriate consumer propagation.
  • Remote machines: plan an explicit sharing method. A path that exists inside DUMB does not automatically become available elsewhere.

The need for propagation comes from the deployment topology, not the workflow's name. Adding :rshared to Compose does not prepare the host mount.

items.title: Ready to deploy
items.text: Choose your deployment guide, start DUMB, and open http://<host>:3005. Then follow onboarding.

items.title: Geek reference
items.text:
Use the frontend guides for everyday tasks. This reference is for understanding the internals or using a different method: configuration files, environment variables, APIs, networking, and process dependencies.

Visual guide: See DUMB's components and storage boundaries.

The frontend workflow remains the main path. These references explain the settings and behavior behind it; they do not add extra required setup steps.

Use these pages to look up exact names and defaults. For a procedure, start with Deployment, Features, or the relevant service guide.

Look up Reference Listener defaults and direct access Service ports Environment variables, Docker secrets, and precedence Environment variables DUMB's configuration format and validation Configuration schema Multiple copies of a supported service Multi-instance configuration Which workflow an Arr instance belongs to Core service routing HTTP and WebSocket endpoints API reference

Defaults describe a fresh configuration. The values saved in /config/dumb_config.json and shown in the dashboard take precedence when diagnosing a running installation.

items.title: Configuration schema
items.text:
DUMB uses a JSON schema to validate /config/dumb_config.json and keep service definitions consistent.

Visual guide: See how settings are read, applied and saved.

items.title: Schema location
items.text:
The default template and schema live in the backend repository/image:

utils/dumb_config.json
utils/dumb_config_schema.json

utils/dumb_config.json is a template; /config/dumb_config.json is the persistent runtime file. On startup DUMB copies the template when needed, adds missing defaults to existing configs, prunes keys removed from the supported template, and validates the result against the schema before creating the effective environment-overridden configuration.

The API exposes the current schema at native GET /config/schema (frontend proxy: GET /api/config/schema) and a process-specific subtree at POST /config/process-config/schema.

items.title: Top-level structure
items.text:
Key Description puid / pgid Container user/group IDs tz Time zone string data_root Base path for persisted data dumb DUMB core settings (API, frontend, logging, tokens) traefik Reverse-proxy configuration traefik_proxy_admin / cloudflared Optional reverse-proxy management and tunnel connector seerr_sync Cross-instance Seerr synchronization postgres / pgadmin Database settings rclone rclone instances and mounts Service keys Core/dependent/optional services (for example decypharr, infinidysk, aiostreams, cli_debrid)

Service blocks are explicit

Each service has its own schema definition (for example decypharr, infinidysk, cli_debrid). This ensures consistent required fields and defaults.

items.title: Validation tips
items.text:
• Validate JSON changes before restart to avoid startup failures.
  • Back up /config/dumb_config.json before large manual edits; use the frontend editor for normal service changes.
  • Keep config_dir, log_file, and port unique for each service instance.
  • Use release_version_enabled for release tags, commit_sha for an exact 40-character GitHub source revision, or branch_enabled for a moving branch.
  • A non-empty commit_sha takes precedence over release and branch settings and disables automatic updates until changed or cleared.
  • Do not edit utils/dumb_config.json expecting a persistent runtime change.

items.title: Related pages
items.text:
• Environment variables
  • Multi-instance configuration

items.title: Core service routing
items.text: core_service is the flag DUMB uses to route automation between Arrs and the core download workflows. It keeps Debrid- and Usenet-based stacks isolated while still allowing multiple instances of the same Arr service.

items.title: Where core_service is used
items.text: Config block Purpose Arr instances (sonarr, radarr, lidarr, whisparr) Selects the download workflow(s) to auto-wire. NeutArr instances Filters which Arr instances are sent to NeutArr. Profilarr instances Filters which Arr instances are auto-linked to Profilarr. rclone/zurg instances Labels the instance for the workflow it supports.

items.title: Routing map
items.text:
%%{ init: { "flowchart": { "curve": "basis" } } }%%
flowchart TD
    ARR[Arr instances]
    CS{core_service}
    DEC[Decypharr Debrid/Usenet workflow]
    NZB[InfiniDysk workflow]
    ALT[AltMount workflow]
    PROWLARR[Prowlarr apps + tags]
    IDX[Tagged indexers]
    NEUTARR[NeutArr instance]
    PROFILARR[Profilarr instance]

    ARR ==> CS
    CS -- decypharr --> DEC
    CS -- infinidysk --> NZB
    CS -- altmount --> ALT
    DEC ==> PROWLARR
    NZB ==> PROWLARR
    ALT ==> PROWLARR
    PROWLARR ==> IDX
    IDX ==> ARR
    CS ==> NEUTARR
    CS ==> PROFILARR

items.title: Supported values
items.text:
Use one or more of the core workflow keys:

Value Workflow Typical use decypharr Debrid and/or Usenet workflow Decypharr torrent and Sabnzbd-compatible Arr clients infinidysk Usenet workflow InfiniDysk + Usenet indexers altmount Usenet workflow AltMount SABnzbd-compatible client + Usenet indexers

Leave core_service empty if you do not want DUMB to auto-wire a service into a workflow. To combine workflows, set core_service to a list or use a comma-separated string.

items.title: What DUMB does with it
items.text:
When core_service is set on an Arr instance, DUMB:

  • Configures matching download clients (Decypharr, InfiniDysk, and/or AltMount).
  • Adds or updates Arr root folders and permissions where that workflow's setup hook owns them. AltMount configures the download-client connection but leaves its import strategy and Arr root folders operator-managed.
  • Creates Prowlarr apps tagged with the same core service(s) so indexers sync only to the intended Arrs.

When core_service combines Decypharr with InfiniDysk or AltMount, DUMB uses the shared /mnt/debrid/combined_symlinks/<slug> base for the Decypharr-owned Arr root. InfiniDysk without Decypharr keeps its InfiniDysk symlink root, and AltMount does not independently rewrite the Arr root folder.

When core_service is set on a NeutArr instance, DUMB:

  • Sends Arr instances whose core services overlap the NeutArr instance.

When core_service is set on a Profilarr instance, DUMB:

  • Auto-links only Arr instances whose core services overlap the Profilarr instance.
  • Seeds profile/custom format/regex/media-management sync for those Arr instances (when use_profilarr is enabled on the Arr).

items.title: Example: split Debrid and Usenet workflows
items.text:
"radarr": {
  "instances": {
    "Debrid": {
      "enabled": true,
      "core_service": "decypharr",
      "use_neutarr": true,
      "use_profilarr": true,
      "port": 7878
    },
    "Usenet": {
      "enabled": true,
      "core_service": "infinidysk",
      "use_neutarr": false,
      "use_profilarr": false,
      "port": 7879
    }
  }
}

In this layout:

  • The Debrid Radarr instance syncs with Decypharr and Debrid indexers.
  • The Usenet Radarr instance links to InfiniDysk because its core_service is infinidysk. Change that field to select another workflow.
  • NeutArr only receives the Debrid instance because use_neutarr is set there.
  • Profilarr only links the Debrid instance because use_profilarr is set there.

items.title: Example: combine workflows on one Arr instance
items.text:
"sonarr": {
  "instances": {
    "Combined": {
      "core_service": ["decypharr", "infinidysk", "altmount"],
      "use_neutarr": true,
      "use_profilarr": true
    }
  }
}

In this layout, DUMB wires Decypharr, InfiniDysk, and AltMount download clients for the same Sonarr instance. Decypharr and InfiniDysk coordinate the DUMB-managed combined root; AltMount's import strategy and compatible Arr paths still need to be reviewed in AltMount.

items.title: Choose the right documentation
items.text:
The selector in the site header switches between Latest release and Development. It shows the DUMB version each channel covers. These numbers refer to DUMB itself, rather than the documentation site's own releases.

The footer shows Documentation release with a separate version number and a link to its release notes. That number identifies the published guides you are reading; it is shared by both channels. Include it when reporting a docs problem. A local or pull-request preview is labelled unreleased instead.

Choose When to use it Latest release You run a stable DUMB image, such as ghcr.io/i-am-puid-0/dumb:latest or a numbered stable tag. Development You run ghcr.io/i-am-puid-0/dumb:dev, or you want to read about work awaiting a stable release.

Switching keeps you on the same guide where it exists. A feature that has not shipped shows an availability page in the release channel with a link to its development guide. If there is no matching page, the selector opens the other channel's homepage.

Check the DUMB version shown in the dashboard's Settings → About if the instructions do not match your installation. The dashboard updates independently: an older dashboard may not show controls supported by its backend, while a newer one cannot add a missing backend feature to an older DUMB image. Check both versions in About. Individually pinned service versions may also differ from the examples.

items.title: Choose the version, then the level of detail
items.text:
The release selector chooses which DUMB behavior the guide describes. Geek mode changes how much of that guide is expanded.

flowchart TD
    Installed["Check DUMB and dashboard versions in Settings → About"] --> Match{"Which DUMB channel do you run?"}
    Match -->|Stable| Released["Header: Latest release"]
    Match -->|Development| Dev["Header: Development"]
    Released --> Read["Follow the ordinary frontend steps"]
    Dev --> Read
    Read --> More{"Want internals or another method?"}
    More -->|Yes| Geek["Enable Geek mode or open one technical section"]
    More -->|No| Task["Complete the task with Geek mode off"]
    Read -. "Reporting a docs issue?" .-> Footer["Include the documentation release from the footer"]

items.title: Use Geek mode when you want more detail
items.text:
The main guide is for people using the DUMB frontend. It explains where to go, what to click or enter, how to save the change, and how to check the result. You should be able to complete that frontend task with Geek mode off.

Geek mode adds two kinds of optional material:

If you want to… Geek sections provide Understand how the feature works Internal processes, dependencies, request/data flow, and detailed workflow diagrams Use another method API calls, command-line tools, environment variables, and manual configuration procedures

For example, the ordinary update guide explains the dashboard's Check for updates, install, and scheduling controls. Its Geek sections explain version selection and the installer lifecycle, with alternative configuration methods.

The header shows On or Off. Enabled Geek sections have a light green background and Geek detail label. Your browser remembers the choice, and you can also open a single section without enabling the whole mode.

Warnings, required frontend steps, deployment guides, community links, and maintainer support remain visible in both modes. A long frontend procedure is still a user procedure; it does not become Geek content because it has many steps.

Some pages have no optional Geek sections. Direct links to a heading inside a closed section open that section so the linked explanation stays reachable. The Geek reference also provides API, configuration, and architecture references directly.

This switch changes the documentation display. It does not change DUMB or its frontend settings. If you see Geek Mode inside the DUMB dashboard, that is a separate setting; see dashboard Settings.

items.title: Spot development additions
items.text:
Each page identifies its documentation channel and DUMB version. Released docs use a blue-green label; Development docs use amber. Words accompany the colors so you can tell them apart without relying on color alone.

In development guides, amber panels and small Dev badges identify additions beyond the released documentation snapshot. A development-only feature page also states which stable DUMB release does not include that feature. A newly written guide for an existing feature is labelled New guide instead.

items.title: How release docs stay current
items.text:
The release channel is a snapshot of reviewed documentation. Later development edits do not silently change its description of the stable image.

A scheduled watcher checks DUMB releases every six hours. When a new stable release matches the reviewed development version and includes the backend source covered by that review, the watcher also checks that the compatible dashboard code has a published stable release. The docs workflow validates and records that snapshot, then Release Please prepares a documentation release. After its checks pass, the generated version update merges automatically and the site publishes from that release's exact source. A maintainer can run the release check or retry publication manually.

If the release version or source does not match the reviewed documentation, promotion stops for a maintainer review. This prevents development features from being presented as released. Shared theme and accessibility fixes can still apply to both channels.

items.title: Documentation for AI agents
items.text: Each channel provides an llms.txt index and llms-full.txt with its complete documentation text. Use the files from the channel matching the installed backend. Technical details are included regardless of the browser's Geek mode preference.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
DUMB reads startup overrides for supported configuration leaf values from environment variables or Docker secrets. Override names follow the existing configuration tree; they do not create new service instances or arbitrary keys. Service subprocess variables are separately defined under each service's env block.

How an override is selected

For each supported leaf key, DUMB uses the highest-priority supplied override. Blank environment values do not replace an existing setting.

flowchart TD
    Key["Supported configuration leaf"] --> Secret{"Docker secret supplied?"}
    Secret -->|Yes| Use["Use the override value"]
    Secret -->|No| Environment{"Nonblank process environment value?"}
    Environment -->|Yes| Use
    Environment -->|No| Dotenv{"Value in /config/.env?"}
    Dotenv -->|Yes| Use
    Dotenv -->|No| Config["Use the saved configuration value"]

items.title: Container variables
items.text:
Variable Default Description PUID 1000 Managed-service user ID; must be greater than 0 PGID 1000 Managed-service group ID; must be greater than 0 TZ unset Time zone (for example America/New_York) DUMB_PNPM_STORE_ROOT /config/.pnpm-store Persistent pnpm package store root used during service setup/builds. Override only if /config is not suitable. DUMB_BUN_CACHE_ROOT /config/.bun-cache Persistent Bun package cache root used during Bun-based service setup/builds, such as Pulsarr. Override only if /config is not suitable. DUMB_YARN_CACHE_ROOT /config/.yarn-cache Persistent Yarn package cache root used during source builds, such as Maintainerr. Override when /config is on slower network storage.

Root IDs are rejected

DUMB's controller starts with the container privileges needed to prepare users, ownership, devices, and mounts, then launches managed services with PUID and PGID. DUMB refuses to start when either value is 0; choose a non-root host user and group that can access the mounted paths.

Complete generated reference

The repository's .env.example is generated from the current config template and contains the complete default set. The table above calls out bootstrap/cache variables operators commonly set directly.

items.title: Config override naming
items.text:
DUMB joins a configuration path with underscores and uppercases it:

Config path Override name puid PUID dumb.github_token DUMB_GITHUB_TOKEN dumb.api_service.host DUMB_API_SERVICE_HOST altmount.port ALTMOUNT_PORT infinidysk.frontend_port INFINIDYSK_FRONTEND_PORT sonarr.instances.Default.port SONARR_INSTANCES_DEFAULT_PORT

List values use valid JSON, such as DUMB_METRICS_FILESYSTEM_PATHS=["/","/mnt/debrid"]. Set dictionary members through their individual leaf names; edit JSON configuration or use the API for structural changes.

items.title: Sources and precedence
items.text:
For a config override named DUMB_API_SERVICE_HOST, DUMB checks:

  1. /run/secrets/DUMB_API_SERVICE_HOST
  2. The process/container environment
  3. /config/.env
  4. The value in /config/dumb_config.json

Blank environment values do not replace configured values. Docker secrets are read as trimmed text and have the highest priority.

InfiniDysk upgrade compatibility

Fresh configurations use the INFINIDYSK_* prefix. Existing deployments may continue supplying legacy NZBDAV_* overrides or Docker secrets; DUMB checks those names as fallbacks until the deployment opts into the canonical persisted identity.

items.title: Service environment variables
items.text:
Each service can define variables passed to that subprocess under its env block in /config/dumb_config.json. These are service runtime variables, not names for overriding DUMB's own config tree.

Example:

"infinidysk": {
  "env": {
    "WEBDAV_USER": "admin",
    "WEBDAV_PASSWORD": "change-me"
  }
}

Secrets in config files

Treat tokens and passwords in dumb_config.json as secrets. Avoid committing them to source control.

items.title: Multi-instance configuration
items.text:
Several DUMB services support multiple instances (for example Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Whisparr, and rclone). This guide shows how to configure instances safely.

Keep each instance separate

The instance name identifies a separate configuration. Ports, native configuration paths and log files must remain distinct.

flowchart TD
    Sonarr["Sonarr instances map"] --> Default["Default instance"]
    Sonarr --> Anime["Anime instance"]
    Default --> First["Its own port, config directory and log"]
    Anime --> Second["A different port, config directory and log"]
    First --> Workflow["Select the intended workflow with core_service"]
    Second --> Workflow

items.title: Instance pattern
items.text:
Services that support instances use an instances map keyed by a friendly name:

"sonarr": {
  "instances": {
    "Default": {
      "enabled": true,
      "process_name": "Sonarr Default",
      "port": 8989,
      "config_dir": "/sonarr/default",
      "config_file": "/sonarr/default/config.xml",
      "log_file": "/sonarr/default/logs/sonarr.txt"
    },
    "Anime": {
      "enabled": true,
      "process_name": "Sonarr Anime",
      "port": 8991,
      "config_dir": "/sonarr/anime",
      "config_file": "/sonarr/anime/config.xml",
      "log_file": "/sonarr/anime/logs/sonarr.txt"
    }
  }
}

items.title: Best practices
items.text:
• Assign unique ports per instance to avoid collisions.
  • Use distinct config_dir and log_file paths.
  • Keep process_name descriptive for clarity in the UI.
  • Set core_service when integrating with Decypharr, InfiniDysk, or AltMount (single value, list, or comma-separated).

items.title: rclone instances
items.text:
rclone also uses an instances map for different mount targets:

"rclone": {
  "instances": {
    "Decypharr": {
      "enabled": true,
      "core_service": "decypharr",
      "mount_dir": "/mnt/debrid",
      "mount_name": "decypharr",
      "config_dir": "/config",
      "config_file": "/config/rclone.conf"
    }
  }
}
